blocks.text: A 58-year-old man who has smoked a pack a day for 35 years and drinks heavily presents with a chronic cough and swollen abdomen. In one patient, two of the most common environmental exposures in the world have been quietly injuring the lungs, vessels and liver for decades. Environmental injury is the study of how agents from outside the body, chemical and physical, damage tissue.

blocks.markdown: Environmental and physical injury covers toxic exposures (tobacco, alcohol, drugs, pollutants), ionising radiation and thermal injury (burns, hypothermia). Each acts through the general mechanisms of cell injury: membrane damage, free radicals, DNA damage and energy failure.

### Tobacco

Tobacco smoke contains thousands of chemicals, including nicotine (addictive, vasoconstrictor), carbon monoxide (binds haemoglobin, reducing oxygen carriage) and carcinogens such as polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons and nitrosamines. Pathological effects of chronic exposure:

- **Respiratory**: chronic bronchitis and **emphysema** (chronic obstructive pulmonary disease), through inflammation and an imbalance of proteases and antiproteases; squamous metaplasia of the bronchial epithelium.
- **Cancer**: lung carcinoma (about 90% of cases are related to smoking), and cancers of the oral cavity, larynx, oesophagus, bladder, pancreas and kidney.
- **Cardiovascular**: accelerated **atherosclerosis**, coronary and peripheral arterial disease, aneurysm, because of endothelial injury, oxidative stress, increased platelet aggregation and carbon monoxide hypoxia.
- **Pregnancy**: low birth weight.

### Alcohol

Ethanol is metabolised mainly in the liver by alcohol dehydrogenase to acetaldehyde (toxic) and then by aldehyde dehydrogenase to acetate; these steps consume NAD+ and increase NADH, which shifts hepatic metabolism toward fat synthesis and away from fatty acid oxidation. Chronic effects:

- **Liver**: the progression is **fatty change (steatosis)**, **alcoholic hepatitis** (hepatocyte swelling, neutrophil infiltrate, Mallory-Denk bodies) and **cirrhosis**. Fatty change is reversible with abstinence; cirrhosis is not.
- **Gastrointestinal**: gastritis, acute and chronic pancreatitis, oesophageal varices (from portal hypertension) and oesophageal cancer.
- **Nervous system**: thiamine deficiency (Wernicke-Korsakoff), cerebellar degeneration, peripheral neuropathy.
- **Heart**: dilated cardiomyopathy. **Fetus**: fetal alcohol syndrome.

Acetaldehyde toxicity, increased NADH, oxidative stress
Fatty liver, alcoholic hepatitis, cirrhosis, pancreatitis, neurological damage
DNA damage directly and via free radicals
blocks.caption: Environmental injuries and their effects.

blocks.title: Alcohol and the liver
blocks.prompt: A man drinks heavily for 15 years. Describe the liver changes in order and which are reversible.

steps.text: Metabolism raises NADH: fatty acid oxidation falls and triglyceride synthesis rises, giving fatty change (steatosis), a reversible stage.
Continued exposure with acetaldehyde and oxidative injury causes hepatocyte necrosis and neutrophilic inflammation: alcoholic hepatitis, with Mallory-Denk bodies.
Chronic injury activates stellate cells, producing fibrosis and regenerative nodules: cirrhosis, which is irreversible.

blocks.markdown:
### Ionising radiation

Ionising radiation (X-rays, gamma rays, particles) has enough energy to eject electrons from atoms. It damages cells by two routes: **direct** damage to DNA (strand breaks, base damage) and **indirect** damage through radiolysis of water, which generates hydroxyl radicals and other reactive oxygen species that attack DNA, membranes and proteins. DNA double-strand breaks are the most important lesion. Consequences depend on dose and cell type: cells may repair the damage, undergo **cell cycle arrest** (p53-dependent), **apoptosis** or **mitotic catastrophe** (death at attempted division), or survive with mutations that can cause cancer later. **Rapidly dividing cells** (bone marrow, intestinal crypt epithelium, gonads, skin) are the most radiosensitive. Late effects include fibrosis and vascular damage, and increased cancer risk (leukaemia, thyroid cancer).

blocks.title: Radiosensitivity
blocks.prompt: After abdominal radiotherapy a patient develops nausea, diarrhoea and low white cell counts within days. Explain.

steps.text: Radiation causes double-strand DNA breaks, directly and through water-derived hydroxyl radicals.
Intestinal crypt cells and bone marrow progenitors divide rapidly, so damaged cells die at mitosis or by p53-mediated apoptosis.
Loss of crypt cells denudes the mucosa (diarrhoea); loss of marrow progenitors reduces white cell output.

blocks.answer: Rapidly dividing tissues are most radiosensitive, giving early gastrointestinal and marrow injury.

blocks.markdown:
### Burns and hypothermia

**Burns**: injury is classified by depth: **superficial** (epidermis only, painful, erythema), **partial thickness** (blisters, painful) and **full thickness** (involves all dermis, leathery and painless because nerve endings are destroyed). Local effects are protein denaturation, coagulative necrosis and increased vascular permeability. Extensive burns (roughly more than 15 to 20% of body surface in adults) cause **systemic effects**: massive fluid loss as exudate and oedema leading to **hypovolaemic shock**, hypoproteinaemia, **infection** (loss of the skin barrier; sepsis is a leading cause of death), hypermetabolism, and later acute kidney injury and respiratory failure (inhalation injury). The area is often estimated by the **rule of nines**.

**Hypothermia** (core temperature below 35 C) slows metabolism and enzyme activity, producing confusion, bradycardia and arrhythmias (including ventricular fibrillation at severe levels) and loss of consciousness. **Local freezing injury** (frostbite) causes ice crystal formation in cells and vascular injury, with thrombosis and tissue necrosis on rewarming.

items: Smoking is the single most important preventable cause of cancer.
Carbon monoxide has about 200 times the affinity for haemoglobin compared with oxygen (commonly quoted approximation).
Rapidly dividing cells are most sensitive to ionising radiation.
Fluid loss and infection are the main systemic threats after extensive burns.

blocks.title: Dose and tissue
blocks.text: The outcome of an environmental injury depends on dose, duration and tissue sensitivity. Chronic low-level exposures (tobacco, alcohol) cause cumulative damage over decades, whereas radiation and burns cause immediate damage proportional to dose and extent.

points: Chronic tobacco exposure causes COPD, lung and other cancers and atherosclerosis; chronic alcohol exposure causes fatty liver, alcoholic hepatitis, cirrhosis, pancreatitis and neurological injury.
Ionising radiation damages DNA directly and through hydroxyl radicals from water radiolysis, and rapidly dividing tissues are most sensitive.
Extensive burns cause hypovolaemic shock, infection and hypermetabolism, and hypothermia causes enzyme slowing and arrhythmias.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a reversible stage of alcoholic liver disease?
questions.explanation: Steatosis can resolve with abstinence, whereas cirrhosis is structurally irreversible. Varices and carcinoma are late complications.

questions.stem: Which of the following correctly pairs a smoking-related cause with its effect?

options.text: Carbon monoxide binding haemoglobin reduces oxygen delivery

questions.correctOptionText: Carbon monoxide binding haemoglobin reduces oxygen delivery
questions.explanation: Carbon monoxide forms carboxyhaemoglobin and reduces oxygen-carrying capacity, contributing to cardiovascular disease. Nicotine is addictive and vasoconstrictive but is not the principal carcinogen.

questions.stem: Ionising radiation damages tissue indirectly mainly through:

options.text: Radiolysis of water producing hydroxyl radicals

questions.correctOptionText: Radiolysis of water producing hydroxyl radicals
questions.explanation: Radiation splits water to produce hydroxyl radicals that damage DNA, membranes and proteins, in addition to direct DNA damage.
Rapidly dividing tissues such as bone marrow, intestinal crypts and gonads are most sensitive because cells with DNA damage die at mitosis.

questions.stem: A man is rescued from a house fire with a painless, leathery, white area on his forearm. Which statement is correct?

options.text: This is a full-thickness burn, painless because dermal nerve endings are destroyed
This is a superficial burn limited to the epidermis
Painlessness means the burn is minor
Full-thickness burns do not risk infection

questions.correctOptionText: This is a full-thickness burn, painless because dermal nerve endings are destroyed

distractorRationale.d: They are at high risk of infection.

questions.explanation: A leathery, white, painless burn indicates destruction of the full dermal thickness, including nerve endings. Loss of the skin barrier carries a high risk of infection.

questions.stem: True or false: The main systemic early threat from extensive burns is loss of fluid from increased vascular permeability, leading to hypovolaemic shock.
questions.explanation: Extensive burns cause leakage of protein-rich fluid into tissues and as exudate, reducing circulating volume. Infection becomes a major later threat.

questions.stem: Using the adult rule of nines (head and neck 9%, each arm 9%, each leg 18%, anterior trunk 18%, posterior trunk 18%, perineum 1%), calculate the percentage of body surface burned in a patient with burns to the whole of the anterior trunk and the whole of the left leg.
questions.explanation: Anterior trunk 18% plus left leg 18% gives 36%. This is a large burn, which would be expected to cause substantial fluid loss and shock.

questions.stem: A man has smoked 20 cigarettes per day (one pack) for 30 years. Calculate his exposure in pack-years (packs per day multiplied by years).
questions.explanation: One pack per day for 30 years is 1 x 30 = 30 pack-years. Pack-years quantify cumulative exposure, which correlates with risk of COPD and lung cancer.

questions.stem: Describe the pathological effects of chronic tobacco smoking on the respiratory and cardiovascular systems.
markingGuide: Chronic bronchitis and emphysema (COPD) from inflammation and protease imbalance
Squamous metaplasia then dysplasia and lung carcinoma; carcinogens (polycyclic hydrocarbons, nitrosamines)
Accelerated atherosclerosis from endothelial injury and oxidative stress
Carbon monoxide reduces oxygen carriage; nicotine causes vasoconstriction
questions.explanation: Smoke acts as irritant, oxidant and carcinogen across multiple organs. The vascular effects arise from endothelial injury and hypoxia.

questions.stem: Explain how ionising radiation damages tissue at the cellular level, and why bone marrow and intestine are particularly vulnerable.
markingGuide: Direct DNA damage: strand breaks, double-strand breaks
Indirect damage: water radiolysis producing hydroxyl radicals and ROS
Cell responses: repair, p53-mediated arrest, apoptosis, mitotic catastrophe, mutation
Rapidly dividing cells (marrow, crypt epithelium) damaged at mitosis
questions.explanation: Double-strand DNA breaks are the key lesion. Tissues with high turnover show earlier and more severe injury.
